name: hydra-record-stage
description: Compose one cycles[].stages[] entry from a stage result and commit it into hydra.json. The record composer for hydra-flows-first-port task 5.2.
$comment: WHAT THIS IS. The supervisor wrote hydra.json by appending to it in shell after each
stage returned. That writer is the last piece of the record path still living outside a
flow: task 2.1 proved a commit can be created entirely over REST (hydra-commit-by-api),
and task 5.1 made a stage result carry its own attribution. This joins them — it takes a
stage result off the item, turns it into the one object hydra's record stores per stage,
and hands it to the commit flow.
WHY EVERY FIELD IS A VALUE AND NEVER A LOOKUP KEY. Task 5.3's guard
(scripts/test-run-reconstructible.sh) fails if any value in the record defers to a
register, flow state or the console — because sequencing state, slot tables and the
console's view are all CACHES, and the moment one of them quietly becomes the only place
a fact lives, the pipeline stops being reconstructible and nobody finds out until a
register is rebuilt. So `owner` is a name, not a user id to resolve; `verdict` is a word,
not a status object to fetch; `exit_code` is the number itself.
WHY THE VERDICT IS COMPUTED HERE AND NOT IN THE NODE. hydra's gate runner uses its exit
code as a failure COUNT, so the workload step returns the number verbatim and refuses to
collapse it. Turning that number into pass/fail is hydra's convention, so it belongs in
hydra's flow — which is also where it stays readable to someone following the pipeline on
a canvas.
WHY THE OUTPUT IS TRUNCATED. A gate run's full output is megabytes and hydra.json is a
committed file. The record keeps the tail, which is where the gate runner prints its
summary line; the full log belongs on the issue comment, which is a different artefact
with a different lifetime.
🔑 WHAT WAS WRONG (REVALIDATION-2026-08-02 D2). `write-record` handed the commit
sub-flow a `config.input` map. `SubFlowNode` has no `input` key and no `output` key —
it reads `flow`/`flowId` and `wait`, and the child is seeded with the parent's ITEMS
(`$this->runs->execute(..., seedItems: $items)`). So the whole map was dead config: the
child never saw `content` or `expectedFiles`, `make-blob` POSTed `{"content": null}`
and GitHub answered 422. The branch tip was byte-identical before and after — the run
'failed' at the very last step, which is the one shape that looks like an outage rather
than a config error.
So the fix is not to pass a map, it is to put the fields ON THE ITEM. Everything
`hydra-commit-by-api` reads — `repo`, `branch`, `path`, `content`, `message`,
`expectedFiles` — is composed here and travels as the item.
⚠️ `read-record` asks for `Accept: application/vnd.github.raw`. The contents API's
default representation is a WRAPPER whose `content` is base64, and the expression
language has no base64 decode (`FlowExpression` ships `toJson`/`fromJson` and no
codec). With the raw media type GitHub returns the file itself, and
`SourceCallNode::decodeBody()` json-decodes any UTF-8 body regardless of content
type — so `record.body` IS the record document.
⚠️ ONE CYCLE ENTRY PER STAGE, and this is a deliberate, documented deviation.
Appending into the LAST element of `cycles[]` cannot be expressed: `SetFieldsNode`
builds objects from DOTTED PATHS and the path is a literal config key, never
templated, so no step can write to `cycles.<n>.stages` for an `n` that depends on the
run; and `compute` is JsonLogic, which evaluates expressions and cannot construct an
object at all. What IS expressible is `merge` — so each stage appends a fresh cycle
entry carrying its own `cycle` number and its one stage. `.cycles[].stages[]` still
enumerates every stage in order, which is exactly what test-run-reconstructible.sh
asks the record, and a reader groups by `cycle` to recover the cycles. Nothing is
lost; the grouping is simply not pre-applied. Closing this properly needs a templated
`set` path or an array-append node in OpenRegister.
⚠️ `refuse-unattributed` used to be `unattributed → unattributed`. A `StopNode` that
receives ZERO items passes through by design (or#2232), so on the ordinary attributed
path the token would land back on its own place and the transition would stay enabled
— the same unbounded-loop shape that killed hydra-analyze-verdicts. It never surfaced
only because the run always died earlier at `write-record`. It now ends on `refused`.

config.$comment: The workload step refuses to run unattributed, so this should never fire. It is here because a record entry with no owner is unfixable AFTER the fact — the run is durable and there is no second chance to ask who ran it. A guard on the last writable moment costs one edge.

`outcome`, `outcome_reason` and `started_at` are CYCLE-level and are computed here because `set` runs before `compute` within a step — the step that builds the cycle object can only template values another step already put on the item. test-run-reconstructible.sh asks the record how the run ENDED and WHEN, and refuses an outcome with no reason: 'an outcome with no reason is a fact you cannot act on'. ⚠️ The three exit-code tests are `===`, not `==`. Under json-logic-php's loose `==` an ABSENT `stage.exitCode` evaluated `null == 0` → TRUE, so a stage that produced no exit code at all was RECORDED as `verdict: pass` / `outcome: passed` / 'every gate passed'. Record-or-die exists so a verdict label cannot advance without a record; a record that invents a pass is worse than none.

One object per stage, every field a VALUE. Dotted keys nest (openregister#2244); `compute` cannot build an object because JsonLogic evaluates expressions rather than constructing them. `failures` is the gate runner's own count, kept beside the verdict because 'fail' alone loses how badly.

Read the CURRENT record before writing, so a stage appends to the cycle rather than replacing it. The commit flow's own tip-moved rail catches a concurrent write; this catches the ordinary case of a second stage in the same cycle. The raw media type is what makes the body usable — see the ⚠️ note at the top of this file.

🔴 `onError` IS `continue` BECAUSE THE FIRST RECORD HAS NOTHING TO READ. On
`stop` this node made the flow able to APPEND to a record and unable to
CREATE one: `openspec/changes/<slug>/hydra.json` does not exist until
something writes it, and a 404 here ended the run before anything did. The
fleet's 398 existing records were all written by the shell hydra, which is
exactly why the gap survived — every path this flow was tried on already had
one.

🔑 A 404 IS THE NORMAL FIRST CASE, not a failure, and everything downstream
already handles it. `append-cycle` guards a null `cycles` (`merge` on null
would write a first cycle that is a hole), and `hydra-commit-by-api` builds
a tree from `base_tree` rather than patching a known blob, so it creates a
new path as readily as it replaces one. This node was the only thing
insisting the file be there.

⚠️ The identity fields in `package-commit` are what a missing record leaves
empty — they used to be copied straight off `record.body`, so a created
record would have carried an empty `app`, `repo`, `issue` and `spec_slug`.
They now coalesce onto the caller's values, which the appending case does
not notice and the creating case depends on entirely.

THE CYCLE NUMBER COMES FROM THE RECORD, NOT FROM THE CALLER.

`append-cycle` used to take `{{cycle}}` off the item, which made the number
whatever the invoking flow happened to pass. The sequencer has no way to know
it — the record is the only thing that knows how many cycles it already holds,
and it has just been read one node earlier. A caller-supplied number would
mean every build claiming to be cycle 1, and the record losing the ordering it
exists to keep.

🔑 IT MUST BE ITS OWN NODE, because `set` runs before `compute` WITHIN a
step. Computing this inside `append-cycle` would evaluate it after the `set`
that consumes it, and `{{cycleNumber}}` would render empty — the same ordering
trap documented on that node and on `package-commit`.

⚠️ `length` on an ABSENT key answers 0, not an error: `is_array(null)` is
false so it falls to `mb_strlen('')`. So a record with no `cycles` yet — the
first build of a change — correctly numbers its first cycle 1 without needing
a guard.

`set` runs before `compute` inside one step, so the cycle entry is built first (dotted paths; `stages.0` becomes a real JSON array because PHP normalises the numeric key) and then merged onto whatever the record already held. The `if` guard matters: `merge` on a null `cycles` would produce `[null]` and write a record whose first cycle is a hole.

🔑 THE FOUR IDENTITY FIELDS ARE RESOLVED HERE RATHER THAN IN
`package-commit`, and the reason is the same ordering rule stated above,
read the other way. Inside one step `set` runs BEFORE `compute`, so a
coalesce written next to the `set` that consumes it would be evaluated too
late — `package-commit` would render `{{recordApp}}` against a key that did
not exist yet and write an empty string. Resolving them in the PREVIOUS
step's `compute` puts the whole thing in front of that `set` with no
intra-step ordering to get wrong.

They coalesce onto values supplied by the CALLER because the record being
read may not exist: `read-record` is `onError: continue` so that a first
record can be created, and on that path `record.body` is absent entirely.
Appending does not notice — the existing record wins every time — and
creating depends on it completely. The sequencer supplies `repoName`,
`repo`, `issueNumber` and `change` under the names read here.

Everything hydra-commit-by-api reads, on the item, because that is the only channel a sub-flow has. `expectedFiles` is 1 and is not a formality: it is the assertion the child's diff-gate checks, and it is the only thing standing between 'my one file landed' and 'my tree quietly reverted four others' (base_tree OVERWRITES). The record identity fields are carried from the record that was just read, so this step never invents them.

⚠️ THEY USED TO READ `record.body` DIRECTLY, which was correct for the only
case this flow could reach: a record that already existed. Now that
`read-record` tolerates a 404 so a FIRST record can be created, `record.body`
is absent on exactly that path — and a template rendering an absent key
yields an empty string rather than failing, so the created record would have
been written with an empty `app`, `repo`, `issue` and `spec_slug`. A record
that exists and identifies nothing is worse than no record: the whole point
of 'the repo is the record' is that it can be READ BACK.

The coalesce happens in `append-cycle`'s `compute`, one step earlier, because
`set` runs before `compute` WITHIN a step — see the note there.
The proved writer (task 2.1): blob -> tree -> commit -> ref, with the tip-moved and compare rails. It is seeded with THIS item, which is why the step above exists.

config.message: A stage result with no owner cannot be recorded: the record answers 'who ran this, on whose credential', and that answer is not recoverable after the run.
